• Problem: earlier SHIFT-WORLD agents cut simulated human–robot conflicts mostly by abstaining, confounding safety claims.
• Key idea: compare intervention policies at exactly matched coverage (40%), so only which interventions are chosen matters.
• Method: gradient-boosted regressor ranks counterfactual advantage of acting vs. yielding, trained on simulator potential-outcome labels.
• Setup: 45k training examples; 5 held-out conditions, 120,000 episodes, 600,000 policy evaluations, 16 paired seeds.
• High intent shift: 63.84% success, 2.52% conflict vs. Commitment heuristic 56.88%, 5.30%.
• Linear counterfactual baseline nearly matches (64.15%, 2.65%): gains come from counterfactual supervision, not nonlinear architecture.
• New: 20–60% budget sweep keeps gains over Commitment; synthetic only, no real-robot or collision guarantees.

• Problem: dodge rate ignores later failures; humanoid can dodge yet fall or leave its allowed area.
• Task success requires dodge, no fall, and pelvis within 1 m of start for four seconds.
• Method: paired camera faults (stale, blank frames) on two fixed G1 depth-dodge policies in simulation.
• Restoring fresh frames at 2 s raises π1 success 50.0% to 95.3%; dodge rate stays 100%.
• Under stale input, π1 dodges then exits area in 121 trials; all exits occur after throw resolution.
• Blank input matches fresh-frame success (same 31/64 rescued), but fresh frames end 0.295 m closer to start.
• Takeaway: report post-encounter motion alongside contact, falls, and area compliance, not dodge rate alone.
